t19: Why does the question "What should we eat?" take twenty minutes? The answer is simple: when options are similar to each other, the brain has no criteria to distinguish them, and decision time stretches not with the value of options but with their similarity. This is exactly where the spinner comes in.
t20: Why do small decisions take so long?
t21: Deciding between options with no real difference between them is cognitively one of the most exhausting things to do. If both restaurants are good, the outcome of choosing one is nearly the same; but as the brain tries to eliminate the possibility of a "wrong choice," the time stretches.
t22: Using a random tool for this kind of decision doesn't make the outcome worse, it just ends the process. Since the difference in a choice that already doesn't matter is irrelevant, making a quick decision is more valuable than making the right decision.
t23: 4 rules for using the spinner correctly
t24: Put only options you'd genuinely accept.
t25: An option you don't want to come up should not be on the spinner.
t26: Keep the number of options between 3–8.
t27: Too many slices make the spinner as exhausting as deciding itself.
t29: Spinning again when you don't like the outcome erases all the benefit of the tool.
t30: Don't use it for big decisions.
t31: The spinner is a speed tool for reversible decisions with revocable outcomes.
t32: Real-world examples of spinners that work in daily life
t33: Dinner: home cooking, ordering in, going out, finish what's left.
t34: Chores: who does dishes, who takes out trash, who goes to the store.
t35: Exercise: walking, running, stretching, rest day.
t36: Movie night: pick a genre, then use a second spinner to pick a movie from that genre.
t37: In class: whose turn it is, which group presents.
t39: Some decisions don't fit in one spinner. For the question "What should we watch?" you need to pick a genre first, then pick a movie within that genre. Nested spinners do exactly that: the result of the first spinner determines the content of the second.
t40: The same logic works for food choice — first the cuisine (Turkish, Italian, Far Eastern), then a dish from that cuisine.
t41: Elimination mode: selecting people in turn
t42: When you want to determine an order instead of making a one-time selection, you use elimination mode: the selected option is removed from the spinner and doesn't come up on the next spin. A practical method for presentation order, game order, or task assignment.
t44: Spinify comes with 14 ready-made spinner templates from food selection to chores; you can also build your own spinner name by name. With features like weighting slices, nested spinners, and elimination mode, the spinner becomes much more than a simple randomizer.
t47: A well-designed spinner gives each slice a probability proportional to its slice width. With equal slices all options have equal probability, with weighted slices they come up in the ratios you set.
t48: Which decisions should I not use a spinner for?
t49: For decisions with irreversible outcomes or long-term effects. The spinner is best for small, reversible decisions where there's no real difference between options.
t50: How many options should I put?
t51: 3 to 8 is ideal. More than that makes reading difficult and brings back the decision-making feeling.
